stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 10, Topic 8.4, The G.I. Bill.
stimulus.text: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the GI Bill, offered returning veterans low-interest loans to buy homes and money to attend college. By the time the original bill expired in 1956, nearly eight million veterans had used its education benefits, out of sixteen million veterans in all. By 1955, the Veterans Administration had backed more than 4.3 million home loans. The benefits reached African American veterans unevenly: states set the rules for extending them, and in Mississippi in 1947 only two of 3,200 VA-backed home loans went to African American veterans.

stem: The GI Bill's greatest long-term effect on American society was which of the following?

options.text: It ended the baby boom by keeping veterans in school
options.misconception: Background from the books: the baby boom grew after the war as veterans married and had children; school aid did not end it.

options.text: It replaced private banks as the main source of home loans
options.misconception: Background from the books: the VA backed loans made by private lenders; it did not replace the banks.

options.text: It moved veterans into homeownership and college, expanding the middle class
It made college free for every American citizen
options.misconception: Background from the books: the bill's school aid went to veterans, not to every citizen.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the baby boom grew as veterans married and had children; the bill's school aid did not stop it.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the VA backed loans that private lenders made; the government did not replace the banks.
rationales.C: Background from the books: millions of veterans bought houses and earned degrees with the bill's help, and homeownership plus a degree are the markers of middle-class life.
rationales.D: Background from the books: only veterans could use the bill's school aid, so college was not made free for every citizen.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what changed for millions of people, not just one veteran: houses bought and degrees earned.
2. Background from the books: eight million veterans used the school aid, and 4.3 million home loans were backed by 1955.
3. Those two gains together lifted working-class veterans into the middle class, which is the long-term change.
Remember: A benefit that reaches millions changes the shape of a class, not just one life.
